story.title: Is Jensen Huang’s job on the line? Yale’s Jeffrey Sonnenfeld estimates it’s “about a 50-50”

facts.text: US tech giant Nvidia is opening a probe into its CEO, Jensen Huang, after reports that Huang was the "target of a foreign intelligence effort," the company's board of directors announced on Sunday.
In his letter to employees, Jensen Huang said, "I love our country and our company.
I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security."
In a letter addressed to Nvidia employees, Huang said that he took "full responsibility" for his actions, while admitting to being unfaithful to his wife and apologising to his family and colleagues.
However, he did not mention the name of the person involved or her reported ties to Beijing.

The board leading the company, which is one of the most valuable in the world, says it has "no reason to believe" that either national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised, but that a thorough independent investigation would be carried out.
The board added that Huang "fully supports the review and has committed to cooperating with it."

China has consistantly rejected the spying allegations, with foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun telling a regular briefing on Monday that "the narrative of a so-called Chinese spy is entirely baseless vilification and smearing."

Last month, The New York Times reported that US intelligence agencies had discovered that Huang had developed close ties with Chinese citizen and chip buyer Alice Huang, and that she was directly sharing information with Beijing.
Its chips power many of the data centres and computing systems used to train and run AI models.
Its advanced chips have also been targeted by US export restrictions to prevent China from getting the latest semiconductor technology.
The question is whether Huang can survive this.

To think through what could come next, this editor spoke Sunday with famed professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, senior associate dean for leadership studies at the Yale School of Management and founder of the Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which has hosted Huang at its CEO summits.
Sonnenfeld likes Huang, he said, and he called Huang’s career salvageable but put the odds at “about a 50-50.” He also had a lot more food for thought.
Nvidia’s board announced Sunday that it’s launching an independent investigation after CEO Jensen Huang told staff he was unfaithful to his wife.
Sonnenfeld noted that Huang’s constant, public advocacy for selling advanced chips to China had already made people anxious.
But if Huang had one, Sonnenfeld continued, removing him would be harder.
Huang may well survive the investigation (Sonnenfeld hopes the board clears him of knowingly aiding anyone).
Sonnenfeld suggested that Huang’s saving grace could be what social psychologists call idiosyncrasy credits , if he can prove he was being duped.
Sonnenfeld expects that even if Huang keeps the title, he’ll have to hand off some of the day-to-day decision-making.
Until now, Huang has been “revered and trusted by everybody in technology,” Sonnenfeld noted.
Yale School of Management's Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, who advises boards on CEO succession, told TechCrunch he estimates it's "about a 50-50" chance Huang remains in his role.

Nvidia's board has launched an investigation into CEO Jensen Huang over his relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative, plunging the world's most valuable chipmaker into a leadership crisis that could reshape the AI industry.
The 50-50 odds Sonnenfeld cited suggest even experts can't predict which way the board will break.
The probe follows revelations that China's Ministry of State Security targeted Huang through a tech executive with close personal ties.

Huang has led Nvidia since co-founding the company in 1993, steering it from a graphics card maker into a $3 trillion colossus that supplies the GPUs behind ChatGPT, Claude, and virtually every major AI system.
Sonnenfeld's 50-50 assessment carries weight.
The board now must weigh whether Huang's relationship with the suspected operative compromised the company's compliance with those restrictions or exposed sensitive technology.
